highlights.content: # TSNBench: Benchmarking LLM Proficiency in Time-Sensitive Networking ### Abstract We present TSNBench, the first benchmark for evaluating large language model (LLM) proficiency in Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN), a suite of IEEE 802.1 standards for deterministic communication with bounded latency in safety-critical domains such as autonomous vehicles, aviation, defense, and industrial automation. While LLMs have been extensively evaluated on general knowledge tasks, their capabilities in safety-critical networking domains remain largely unexplored. TSNBench comprises 939 expert-validated multiple-choice questions (MCQs) covering diverse TSN mechanisms, along with 100 open-ended Worst-Case Delay (WCD) computation tasks for Credit-Based Shaper (CBS) and Cyclic Queuing and Forwarding (CQF) across varying network topologies and traffic conditions. MCQ answers are validated by domain experts, and open-ended ground truth WCD values are computed using a verified Network Calculus (NC) solver for CBS and closed-form mathematical upper bounds for CQF. We evaluate 16 LLMs and find that although models achieve 67 to 95\\% accuracy on MCQs, they fail substantially on open-ended WCD computation. For CBS, only GPT-5 achieves a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 36.2\\%, meaning its predicted WCD deviates by 36.2\\% of the actual TSN flow delay on average, while most models exceed 80\\%. For CQF, the best model achieves 41.8\\% MAPE, with most models clustering between 80\\% and 100\\%. Such errors are large relative to TSN latency budgets and can lead to violations of real-time constraints and unsafe configurations. TSNBench demonstrates that MCQ benchmarks may overestimate LLM capabilities in safety-critical networking domains.

highlights.content: # Beyond the Hype: 6 Mind-Bending Takeaways About the Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol ## Introduction: The Agent Tower of Babel The artificial intelligence landscape is experiencing an unprecedented surge in autonomous AI agents. Developers and enterprise engineering teams are building specialized agents across a fragmented web of frameworks — ranging from LangGraph, CrewAI, and Semantic Kernel to Google’s Agent Development Kit (ADK) and custom in-house codebases. While these agents excel at executing local decisions, perceiving isolated environments, and performing task-specific actions, a critical architectural bottleneck has emerged: how do independent AI agents communicate and delegate tasks without requiring custom, point-to-point glue code for every single integration? Consider a complex workflow like automated travel management. Fulfilling an end-user request requires an overarching trip planner agent to coordinate with a flight booking agent, a hotel reservation agent, and a local excursion agent. If every agent framework relies on proprietary communication interfaces, building cross-system workflows becomes prohibitively expensive, fragile, and unscalable. Swapping out a hotel agent for a third-party vendor’s alternative requires re-engineering custom API integrations from scratch. This interoperability challenge — the “Agent Tower of Babel” — is precisely what the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol solves. Initially introduced by Google in April 2025 and now housed under neutral governance by the Linux Foundation within the Agentic AI Foundation under an Apache 2.0 open-source license, A2A provides an open, universal standard. It serves as a common language for opaque agentic applications to dynamically discover one another, negotiate security capabilities, delegate sub-tasks, stream rich media, and orchestrate complex multi-agent workflows across enterprise boundaries. ## 1: A2A and MCP Are Teammates, Not Rivals A persistent misconception in the developer community is that the Agent2Agent protocol competes directly with Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP). In reality, A2A and MCP address two entirely distinct layers of the modern agentic stack, operating as complementary teammates rather than rivals. - **MCP (Model Context Protocol):** Operates at the agent-to-resource layer. It standardizes how an individual agent connects to its local tools, external APIs, databases, and context repositories — effectively standardizing function calling and tool execution. - **A2A (Agent2Agent Protocol):** Operates at the agent-to-agent layer. It standardizes peer-to-peer interaction between independent agents, enabling them to discover capabilities, delegate complex multi-step tasks, and negotiate multi-turn workflows across distinct system boundaries. In a sophisticated agentic architecture, agents rely on MCP to interact with their underlying tools and database engines, while using A2A to discover, negotiate, and delegate tasks to peer agents across enterprise ecosystems. “MCP is all about how an agent connects to its tools, APIs, and resources… A2A, on the other hand, facilitates dynamic communication between different independent agents acting as peers… So you’ll often see both in a sophisticated agentic system. Agents use A2A to coordinate with other agents, and they use MCP to interact with their tools to get part of the job done.” — Holt Skinner, Developer Advocate, Google Cloud AI ## 2: Opacity is a Security Feature, Not a Bug Early multi-agent research frameworks often relied on open-state architectures, where collaborating agents shared full prompt histories, joint memory stores, or raw vector contexts. While this works in isolated sandbox experiments, sharing internal states across organizational boundaries in enterprise B2B environments is an absolute non-starter. highlights.content: ![](https://sb.scorecardresearch.com/p?c1=2&c2=39636245&cv=3.9.1&cj=1) # Nvidia’s AI Money Machine Keeps Churning Without Jensen Huang Reading time 2 minutes ![Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at GTC Berlin](https://gizmodo.com/app/uploads/2026/11/former-ceo-huang.jpg) Nvidia wants you to know that no matter the scandals, the money will keep flowing. Nvidia reported $115.84 billion in revenue in its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday evening, beating market [expectations](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-nvda-earnings-report-q3-2027.html) and more than doubling since last year. The company [said](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-nvda-earnings-report-q3-2027.html) that it forecasts revenue to continue growing to roughly $130 billion in the next quarter, without assuming any revenue from data-center compute sales in China. The earnings results are Nvidia’s first since co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, who led the company for the past 33 years, resigned last week. Huang’s reputation has been battered by reports that he had engaged in three separate affairs: two with Nvidia employees, and one with a woman whose suspected ties to Chinese intelligence are under investigation by U.S. authorities. Chief financial officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO while the board finds Huang’s successor, even though a group of employees, fellow tech chiefs, President Trump, and [even Huang himself](https://gizmodo.com/jensen-huang-says-hed-be-honored-to-return-as-nvidia-ceo-2000841098) have expressed a desire to see the disgraced CEO reinstated. Nvidia’s newly appointed board chairman, Harvey Jones, said during the earnings call that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On the earnings call on Tuesday, Kress assured investors that the eye-popping growth projections promised by Huang would continue on without him. “Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change,” Kress said in the earnings call on Tuesday. Nvidia’s financial results have repercussions for the entire AI industry. As the chief infrastructure supplier of the AI industry, the chipmaker sits atop a precarious web of dealmaking that some experts have deemed to be circular. Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning ###### Abstract Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with *counterfactual views*, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision–language accuracy by 46.1–53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model’s answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: <https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/>. ## 1 Introduction Multimodal signals in the wild are rarely complete, and the causes that corrupt test data corrupt training data as well. Most incomplete multimodal learning (IML) methods reconstruct the missing modalities [[60](#bib.bib60), [55](#bib.bib55), [28](#bib.bib28), [45](#bib.bib45), [44](#bib.bib44)] or distil from a complete-modality teacher [[27](#bib.bib27), [50](#bib.bib50)], and therefore still need complete training observations. Large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative: modality features enter as token blocks, missing modalities become learnable placeholders, and a prompt describes availability. We study such *LLM-driven fusion* under dynamic modality masking, with a pattern sampled at each training visit. Yet these models still fail on cases that are elementary for a human. In the clips of , a speaker sarcastically says “there’s no place I would rather be than here”, and a child announces with a beaming smile that grandpa has come to scold their father. AI Agents.content: # Beyond the Hype: 6 Mind-Bending Takeaways About the Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol ## Introduction: The Agent Tower of Babel The artificial intelligence landscape is experiencing an unprecedented surge in autonomous AI agents. Developers and enterprise engineering teams are building specialized agents across a fragmented web of frameworks — ranging from LangGraph, CrewAI, and Semantic Kernel to Google’s Agent Development Kit (ADK) and custom in-house codebases. While these agents excel at executing local decisions, perceiving isolated environments, and performing task-specific actions, a critical architectural bottleneck has emerged: how do independent AI agents communicate and delegate tasks without requiring custom, point-to-point glue code for every single integration? Consider a complex workflow like automated travel management. Fulfilling an end-user request requires an overarching trip planner agent to coordinate with a flight booking agent, a hotel reservation agent, and a local excursion agent. If every agent framework relies on proprietary communication interfaces, building cross-system workflows becomes prohibitively expensive, fragile, and unscalable. Swapping out a hotel agent for a third-party vendor’s alternative requires re-engineering custom API integrations from scratch. This interoperability challenge — the “Agent Tower of Babel” — is precisely what the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol solves. Initially introduced by Google in April 2025 and now housed under neutral governance by the Linux Foundation within the Agentic AI Foundation under an Apache 2.0 open-source license, A2A provides an open, universal standard. It serves as a common language for opaque agentic applications to dynamically discover one another, negotiate security capabilities, delegate sub-tasks, stream rich media, and orchestrate complex multi-agent workflows across enterprise boundaries. ## 1: A2A and MCP Are Teammates, Not Rivals A persistent misconception in the developer community is that the Agent2Agent protocol competes directly with Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP). In reality, A2A and MCP address two entirely distinct layers of the modern agentic stack, operating as complementary teammates rather than rivals. - **MCP (Model Context Protocol):** Operates at the agent-to-resource layer. It standardizes how an individual agent connects to its local tools, external APIs, databases, and context repositories — effectively standardizing function calling and tool execution. - **A2A (Agent2Agent Protocol):** Operates at the agent-to-agent layer. It standardizes peer-to-peer interaction between independent agents, enabling them to discover capabilities, delegate complex multi-step tasks, and negotiate multi-turn workflows across distinct system boundaries. In a sophisticated agentic architecture, agents rely on MCP to interact with their underlying tools and database engines, while using A2A to discover, negotiate, and delegate tasks to peer agents across enterprise ecosystems. “MCP is all about how an agent connects to its tools, APIs, and resources… A2A, on the other hand, facilitates dynamic communication between different independent agents acting as peers… So you’ll often see both in a sophisticated agentic system. Agents use A2A to coordinate with other agents, and they use MCP to interact with their tools to get part of the job done.” — Holt Skinner, Developer Advocate, Google Cloud AI ## 2: Opacity is a Security Feature, Not a Bug Early multi-agent research frameworks often relied on open-state architectures, where collaborating agents shared full prompt histories, joint memory stores, or raw vector contexts. There is a clear need for autonomous analytical solutions that can utilize recent advancements in agentic AI such as agent harnessing and loop engineering without introducing hallucination or workflow fragmentation. Researchers, regardless of technical expertise, need tools that streamline complex data analysis and deliver meaningful, actionable insights grounded in both data and established biomedical knowledge. EcoXAI addresses this by introducing a modular, customizable, containerized multi-agent system that structures analysis into explicit pipeline execution stages, lowering the computational barrier for clinical and translational researchers. Result: EcoXAI replaces monolithic AI text interfaces with an autonomous execution-driven framework with specialized bioinformatics agents for delivering proactive, data-driven insights grounded in established biological knowledge. Unlike purely LLM-driven or less integrated AI solutions prone to hallucinations or biologically implausible outcomes, EcoXAI’s multi-agent framework, which leverages modern agentic management and explicit knowledge graph integration, provides greater transparency and verifiability in its reasoning. In our use case in drug repurposing for Alzheimer’s Disease, EcoXAI evaluated 103 drug candidates and identified 79 novel candidates whose predictive models exceeded a randomized baseline, including the CCR5 antagonist Maraviroc, whose generated hypothesis was subsequently supported by the literature. These results demonstrate the potential of knowledge graph-grounded AI agents to accelerate hypothesis-driven biomedical research. Below, under "Any browser-based system," are the logos of SAP, Oracle Fusion, Workday, Coupa, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and more.](https://www.salesforce.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/Bridget.png?w=888) Bridget connects your systems without code, then does the manual work inside them. Generally available in Regrello Nov. 18 and expected in MuleSoft in December. ![](https://www.salesforce.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Jason-Briggs.png?w=150) ## Share article Picture this scenario: A supplier is approved, the documents are complete, and procurement is ready to place the order. But before that can happen, a person must log into the supplier-management system, work through dozens of screens, and manually enter information the business should already know. At many companies, the order waits and the work slips. Cycle times stretch, operating costs rise, and contracts and revenue are put at risk. For decades, IT has gone to great lengths to integrate enterprise applications and automate approvals. But critical work still happens manually in the core systems that run the business — step by step, screen by screen, click by click. This problem is common in the [middle and back office](https://www.salesforce.com/blog/regrello/) where work often moves at the speed of human-first processes. In finance and supply chain, for example, suppliers need to be onboarded, orders processed, and records kept current across systems. The final step in these processes is usually a person logging in and entering the data by hand. This tedious, manual drag is known as the last mile of a business process. [AI agents](https://www.salesforce.com/agentforce/what-are-ai-agents/) hit the same barrier when they don’t have access to a system. When an agent can’t complete the next step in an application, the task goes back to a person. Meet Bridget, your headless systems integration agent. She quickly connects systems without code, then does the manual work inside your core applications herself. There’s no long, costly integration project to add to the IT backlog. Business teams can improve their own processes and move faster, while IT maintains oversight. With Bridget generally available in [Regrello](https://www.salesforce.com/agentforce/regrello/) on Nov. 18, companies can now turn human-first processes into AI-first operations. LLMs.titleZh: NeurIPS Poster TSNBench: Benchmarking LLM Proficiency in Time-Sensitive Networking
LLMs.content: # TSNBench: Benchmarking LLM Proficiency in Time-Sensitive Networking ### Abstract We present TSNBench, the first benchmark for evaluating large language model (LLM) proficiency in Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN), a suite of IEEE 802.1 standards for deterministic communication with bounded latency in safety-critical domains such as autonomous vehicles, aviation, defense, and industrial automation. While LLMs have been extensively evaluated on general knowledge tasks, their capabilities in safety-critical networking domains remain largely unexplored. TSNBench comprises 939 expert-validated multiple-choice questions (MCQs) covering diverse TSN mechanisms, along with 100 open-ended Worst-Case Delay (WCD) computation tasks for Credit-Based Shaper (CBS) and Cyclic Queuing and Forwarding (CQF) across varying network topologies and traffic conditions. MCQ answers are validated by domain experts, and open-ended ground truth WCD values are computed using a verified Network Calculus (NC) solver for CBS and closed-form mathematical upper bounds for CQF. We evaluate 16 LLMs and find that although models achieve 67 to 95\\% accuracy on MCQs, they fail substantially on open-ended WCD computation. For CBS, only GPT-5 achieves a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 36.2\\%, meaning its predicted WCD deviates by 36.2\\% of the actual TSN flow delay on average, while most models exceed 80\\%. For CQF, the best model achieves 41.8\\% MAPE, with most models clustering between 80\\% and 100\\%. Such errors are large relative to TSN latency budgets and can lead to violations of real-time constraints and unsafe configurations. TSNBench demonstrates that MCQ benchmarks may overestimate LLM capabilities in safety-critical networking domains.

We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with *counterfactual views*, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision–language accuracy by 46.1–53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model’s answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Microsoft stated that compared with the previous generation model, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 features stronger intelligence, more accurate calibration capability, **over 2 times higher operation speed and lower cost**. Apart from decision-making models, Microsoft also launched the programming model MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash tailored for enterprises' daily coding tasks, as well as new models Code 2 and Code 2 Flash built specifically for programming and cybersecurity at the Ignite conference. Among them, in three coding benchmark tests measuring daily high-volume regular coding tasks, the performance of MAI Code 2 Flash is comparable to that of GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, with the cost being only 65% and 20% of theirs respectively. The new-generation decision-making model adds multi-modal support and can receive images. In terms of pricing, in Microsoft Foundry, it costs **$0.042 per million input tokens**, with outputs free of charge. Microsoft stated that its decision-making models are designed to make calibrated decisions under the uncertainty of various real-world software use cases. LLMs.titleZh: Study Finds AI Chatbots Fail Reading Benchmarks for Melanoma Education
LLMs.content: A cross-sectional comparative investigation published in Frontiers in Public Health has revealed that while contemporary artificial intelligence chatbots can answer melanoma-related medical examination questions with remarkable accuracy, their written explanations remain too linguistically complex for the general public and consistently lack foundational transparency regarding their sources. Conducted by an interdisciplinary team of clinical researchers from Central South University and the University of South China, the study evaluated four leading conversational platforms: ChatGPT-5.6, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 5, and DeepSeek-V4. The researchers discovered that despite differences in medical knowledge precision, not a single evaluated model generated patient-oriented guidance that conformed to the sixth-grade reading level standard universally recommended for consumer health information. The clinical motivation behind the evaluation stems from the rapid surge in consumer reliance on generative artificial intelligence for personal medical inquiries alongside the growing global burden of melanoma. According to GLOBOCAN 2022 epidemiological data cited by the investigators, approximately 330,000 newly diagnosed melanoma cases and nearly 60,000 associated deaths occurred worldwide in 2022, with international forecasts projecting an increase to roughly 510,000 annual cases and 96,000 fatalities by 2040 if current incidence trends continue unchecked. However, previous assessments of digital resources have demonstrated that patient-facing melanoma websites consistently display wide variations in clinical reliability while averaging a college-level reading grade of 12.6, far exceeding recommended thresholds. To rigorously determine whether conversational generative models solve or replicate these health communication barriers, the investigators established an objective two-part methodology that combined standardized professional knowledge testing with evaluations of authentic public inquiries. In the first phase, response validity was tested using a curated bank of 200 single-best-answer multiple-choice questions. This diagnostic test suite comprised 30 questions derived from the Medical Question Answering dataset, 137 questions from the Medical Multiple-Choice Question Answering dataset, and 33 questions drawn from Chinese national medical qualification examinations. The collection encompassed etiology, pathological hallmarks, anatomical presentations, and therapeutic strategies, with all answer keys independently verified by two clinicians against standard medical references without discrepancy. To evaluate the chatbots under strict, reproducible conditions, each of the 200 examination questions was submitted independently across three separate trials to each chatbot through its standard official web interface, utilizing default parameter configurations without active web browsing or retrieval augmentation. Across these 600 total query administrations per platform, ChatGPT-5.6 achieved the highest mean accuracy at 94.0 percent with a standard deviation of 0.5 percent, corresponding to an error rate of 6.0 percent. Gemini 3.5 Flash followed closely with an overall mean accuracy of 92.5 percent and an error rate of 7.5 percent. AI Product.titleZh: Microsoft Accelerates In-House AI Push, Unveils Multiple Specialized Models at Ignite Conference | NAI 500
AI Product.content: Microsoft (MSFT) has achieved a milestone in its in-house AI development through specialized AI models, leveraging cost advantages to attract enterprise customers while continuing to advance general-purpose large models. The market will continue to watch two things: first, whether the technical accumulation in specialized models can be rapidly translated into competitiveness in general-purpose large models; second, whether the price advantage can attract customers to migrate. Mustafa Suleyman, head of Microsoft AI, said the company has made significant progress in developing its own frontier general-purpose AI models, and at the Ignite conference it released six specialized AI models that can achieve performance comparable to mainstream products from OpenAI and Anthropic at far lower cost, with some tasks that previously took weeks now completable in just minutes. For a long time, Microsoft’s high-end AI models have mainly relied on supplies from external companies such as OpenAI. This product launch marks Microsoft’s ability to offer competitive in-house models and reflects the company’s intention to actively participate in market competition on price. The six new models cover coding, cybersecurity, image generation, speech transcription and other areas. Among them, MAI Code 2, as the flagship coding model, approaches top competitors in performance with outstanding cost advantages; MAI Code 2 Flash focuses on lightweight design and speed; MAI Cyber 2 Flash targets cybersecurity scenarios, and Microsoft plans to open this model to limited customers to address the growing number of software vulnerabilities. Among the other new products, MAI Image 2.7 performs strongly in image editing scenarios, and the new speech model also targets industry leaders. The starting point of Microsoft’s strategy is to ease the growing token expenditure pressure on enterprise customers. The team chose to focus on specific scenarios to build specialized models that carry more knowledge and professional capabilities at the same parameter count, continuously optimizing performance and pricing. The approach also has limitations: scenario-specific models are weaker in general tasks such as mathematics and scientific research, performance comparisons are based on selected benchmarks, and part of the low price comes from promotional discounts. In addition to the models, Microsoft also introduced the Microsoft IQ platform, Copilot Fusion and intelligent model selection features at the conference to help enterprises accumulate internal knowledge, flexibly schedule models and control invocation costs. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Copilot Fusion can chain multiple models together to deliver high-quality results at lower cost. At the same time, OpenAI also updated its models and cut prices, intensifying industry competition. Suleyman revealed that Microsoft’s pretraining and reinforcement learning of general-purpose foundation models are progressing well, but did not disclose a launch date. These in-house models may change Microsoft’s partnership landscape with service providers such as OpenAI, as MAI Code 2 will be integrated into GitHub Copilot, offloading some of the workload from external models. Microsoft is also opening model weight licensing to enterprise customers, who can fine-tune models based on their own data, but the models must be deployed on the Azure platform. Security alignment is also a research priority, and recent security incidents caused by AI agents have led the team to place greater emphasis on constraining harmful AI behavior. Nadella also responded at the conference to a previous cross-regional service outage, saying the company will continue to optimize services and maintain customer trust. On the trading side, Microsoft’s stock closed down 2.27% on Tuesday and has risen 5.3% year to date, underperforming the S&P 500 index, and was up 0.9% in after-hours trading as of press time.

AI Product.titleZh: Wonder Unveils AI-Powered Restaurant Builder as Marc Lore Pushes Toward a Fully Automated Food Business
AI Product.content: # Wonder Unveils AI-Powered Restaurant Builder as Marc Lore Pushes Toward a Fully Automated Food Business Marc Lore’s food-tech startup Wonder unveiled a tool that uses AI to create restaurant concepts, menus, recipes, branding, and marketing materials. The launch comes days after the company disclosed it had confidentially filed paperwork to go public. BY JENNIFER CONRAD, SENIOR WRITER @JENNIFERCONRAD Marc Lore. Illustration: Inc.; Photos: Courtesy Wonder Marc Lore clearly doesn’t believe the “slop-bowl apocalypse” is upon us. His multi-restaurant food-delivery platform Wonder, which recently filed confidential paperwork to go public, today unveiled its AI-powered restaurant creation tool Wonder Create. It’s an early step in what he sees as a fully autonomous, robot-powered meal development, preparation, and delivery service. Wonder’s core business is a chain of about 170 ghost kitchens that offer delivery and takeout meals from multiple restaurants, including those Wonder incubated in house, developed with well-known chefs, or acquired. The idea is that diners can choose from multiple “restaurants” in a single order, with all of the food prepared and delivered out of a single location. With Wonder Create, the company is taking that concept even further, allowing people to build their own virtual restaurants with meals that can be ordered on Wonder. The platform’s AI tools will develop the name, logo, concept, photography, and product descriptions. The AI will also develop the recipes for any dish that can be made in Wonder’s specialized bowl-making machines using a set of 130 ingredients. It costs $10 a month to sign up, and the user determines the profit margin they want to make and takes a cut from each sale. ## Your own personal restaurant The first thing users can generate? Personalized bowls, salads, and poke bowls like those found at chains including Sweetgreen, Cava, and Chop’t, the latter of which is partnering with Wonder to trial new dishes and expand to new markets using Create. The daily digest for entrepreneurs and business leaders Lore says the platform will enable anyone to set up their own restaurant concepts in minutes. “You basically go in there and you say ‘build me a fast casual Mexican concept for Gen Z, for people who love World Cup’…and then you hit go,” Lore said, describing Wonder Create at a fireside chat with Inc. editor-in-chief Mike Hofman during the Inc. 5000 conference in October. Celebrities and athletes—including entrepreneur Gary Vaynerchuk, talk show host Andy Cohen, and the gymnast-turned-model Livvy Dunne—will have their own Wonder Create restaurants listed on the Wonder platform. Nonprofits such as the Ronald McDonald House New York and Food Bank for New York City will also have their own concepts on the platform, with the proceeds supporting their missions. Creators looking for new ways to make money from their followings can sign up, and the company says nearly 1,000 are already on the waitlist. But Lore says he expects that most users will be people with specialized diets, such as his own gluten-free, dairy-free, grain-free, high-protein diet. “These are the 20 menu items that I created for myself based on my dietary habits, my food preferences, my intolerances, the right micro macronutrients,” he says, describing how someone might build their concept. “It’s like the perfect restaurant for you.”

The investment reflects growing demand for AI-driven security tools as attackers increasingly use automation, though Corma must still prove its technology’s effectiveness against established competitors. U.S. company Corma, which develops AI systems to defend against cyberattacks, has raised $125 million in a Series A funding round at a $1 billion valuation. Notably, only about three months have passed since its product's public launch. The startup's rapid success shows how quickly investor interest is growing in technologies capable of countering new threats that artificial intelligence itself is helping to create, TechCrunch reports. ## **A billion-dollar valuation after just a few months in operation** Corma emerged from stealth in August 2026, introducing models and AI agents specifically trained for cybersecurity tasks. By November, the company had announced a $125 million Series A round led by investment firm NEA. The latest round brings Corma's total funding to $185 million. The startup's investors also include Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue. A billion-dollar valuation just a few months after a product launch indicates how high expectations currently are for AI in information security. Companies and government organizations face a growing number of threats, while traditional security tools cannot always keep pace with the speed and scale of modern attacks. ## **One day that revealed the scale of the problem** The sharp rise in interest in Corma coincided with a series of cybersecurity incidents. October 21 was particularly telling: on that day, several serious vulnerabilities and security issues drew experts' attention and forced information security leaders to respond urgently to threats. A critical vulnerability was discovered in PHP, a popular programming language for web development. Another issue was identified in Node.js, a JavaScript runtime widely used to build server-side applications. On the same day, a security incident was reported by LiteLLM, a popular open-source tool that routes requests between different large language model providers. This is a particularly sensitive area: such tools are becoming part of the infrastructure of AI services and can create additional entry points for attacks. These events demonstrated an unsettling feature of the current stage of technological development: artificial intelligence is expanding the capabilities not only of security professionals but also of potential attackers. Automation makes it possible to find vulnerabilities faster, scale attacks, and exploit software flaws. ## **AI versus AI: a new cybersecurity market** Corma is far from the only company trying to use artificial intelligence to counter such threats. Both young startups and major technology players are working in this area. New ventures include Armadin, a startup founded by Kevin Mandia, the former head of cybersecurity company Mandiant. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Microsoft are also developing their own solutions in this field. However, the market is still young, and the number of companies trying to carve out a place in it is growing rapidly. Corma positions itself not simply as a security software developer b...

Infra & Chips.content: ![](https://sb.scorecardresearch.com/p?c1=2&c2=39636245&cv=3.9.1&cj=1) # Nvidia’s AI Money Machine Keeps Churning Without Jensen Huang Reading time 2 minutes ![Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at GTC Berlin](https://gizmodo.com/app/uploads/2026/11/former-ceo-huang.jpg) Nvidia wants you to know that no matter the scandals, the money will keep flowing. Nvidia reported $115.84 billion in revenue in its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday evening, beating market [expectations](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-nvda-earnings-report-q3-2027.html) and more than doubling since last year. The company [said](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-nvda-earnings-report-q3-2027.html) that it forecasts revenue to continue growing to roughly $130 billion in the next quarter, without assuming any revenue from data-center compute sales in China. The earnings results are Nvidia’s first since co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, who led the company for the past 33 years, resigned last week. Huang’s reputation has been battered by reports that he had engaged in three separate affairs: two with Nvidia employees, and one with a woman whose suspected ties to Chinese intelligence are under investigation by U.S. authorities. Chief financial officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO while the board finds Huang’s successor, even though a group of employees, fellow tech chiefs, President Trump, and [even Huang himself](https://gizmodo.com/jensen-huang-says-hed-be-honored-to-return-as-nvidia-ceo-2000841098) have expressed a desire to see the disgraced CEO reinstated. Nvidia’s newly appointed board chairman, Harvey Jones, said during the earnings call that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On the earnings call on Tuesday, Kress assured investors that the eye-popping growth projections promised by Huang would continue on without him. “Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change,” Kress said in the earnings call on Tuesday. Kress said that the company was now expecting revenue to grow “approximately 75%” in the next fiscal year, beating a previous 70% forecast that had shocked and delighted investors when the chip giant reported second quarter earnings [back in August.](https://gizmodo.com/nvidia-tries-to-defend-against-circular-dealmaking-accusations-2000803583) According to a recent [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/colette-kress-cfo-who-challenged-huangs-bets-is-nvidias-interim-ceo-2026-11-13/) report, Kress clashed with Huang over some of Nvidia’s aggressive financing decisions, which fed [the circular-dealmaking accusations](https://gizmodo.com/nvidia-tries-to-defend-against-circular-dealmaking-accusations-2000803583) the company has spent much of the last year trying to refute. Nvidia’s financial results have repercussions for the entire AI industry. As the chief infrastructure supplier of the AI industry, the chipmaker sits atop a precarious web of dealmaking that some experts have deemed to be circular. Through several multibillion-dollar deals with top companies across the AI industry like OpenAI and the [soon-to-IPO Anthropic](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivenvidia-in-talks-to-invest-in-anthropics-mega-ipo-sources-say-4898552), Nvidia’s role in the AI buildout has evolved from infrastructure provider to one of [its biggest financiers.](https://gizmodo.com/top-wall-street-firms-reportedly-partnering-with-nvidia-for-500b-ai-investment-2000796682) Critics warn that these arrangements create [financial dependencies](https://gizmodo.com/googles-flashy-new-model-gets-outshone-by-its-financial-troubles-2000832147), raising the possibility that trouble at one major company or the collapse of a significant deal could ripple through the industry, with [potentially serious consequences for the broader market](https://gizmodo.com/big-short-investor-expects-ai-bubble-burst-sooner-than-later-2000818889). ![](https://gizmodo.com/app/themes/gizmodo/public/images/n...

Working with Amkor Technology, Foxconn, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, [Samsung Electro-Mechanics](https://samsungsem.com/global/newsroom/news/overview.do), Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and TSMC, NVIDIA is expanding manufacturing capacity across substrates, advanced packaging, wafer and contract manufacturing to scale production of its current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. “Our supply chain is a strategic advantage,” said Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations at NVIDIA. “Our work with these partners builds on our manufacturing foundation for long-term growth, expanding capacity across components, advanced packaging and system production to deliver the accelerated computing platforms our customers need.” **Increasing Substrate Capacity and Production Capabilities** NVIDIA is expanding its substrate supply commitments with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics, adding manufacturing capacity and improving production capabilities at existing factories. Under a new agreement with NVIDIA, Kinsus plans to expand its advanced ABF package substrate manufacturing capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by more than 3.5x over current levels from its Youth campus in Taoyuan, Taiwan. Production is expected to begin in the second half of 2027, with the additional capacity targeted for the third quarter of 2028. This multiyear agreement builds on the companies’ existing supplier relationship and supports NVIDIA’s long-term supply planning for its accelerated computing platforms. “We believe AI will be one of the most important technology transitions of our lifetime,” said Scott Chen, CEO and president of Kinsus. “After more than a decade of partnership with NVIDIA, we are excited to continue building the future together.” NVIDIA and Samsung Electro-Mechanics have amended their existing substrate supply agreement to improve operational capabilities at existing factories in support of increased production of NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platforms.
